Mr. Speaker, in supporting the amendment I do not believe we have destroyed or altered the policy as expressed in the original resolution. We are simply phrasing it in language which appears to us to make it more practicable. I might have very little to say on this subject had it not been for the fact that the hon. member for Qu'Appelle (Mr. Millar) fears that we are in some way interfering with or destroying the influence of the pension board. This motion and its amendment do not in any way destroy or interfere with the pension board. The pension board simply administers the wish of the house as expressed by certain legislation. It cannot alter, change or interfere one iota with that legislation; it only administers the law, interprets it as it sees it. That does not interfere with the house or its committee in any way in expressing the spirit of the house in regard to the legislation that is placed before it. I would appeal to the hon. member for Qu'Appelle to change his opinion in regard to the amendment and the motion. We have a right to legislate, and it is within our province to give expression to the spirit which we believe should underly legislation for which parliament is responsible.
In reference to the particular matter under consideration I would like to draw attention to the fact that time and again this spirit has been expressed in committee meetings. We have had promise after promise from representatives of the pension board that attention would be given to these matters. That has not been done and it only remains for the
house by motion to place itself on record upon this question. I would like to take the members of the committee and of the house back to certain meetings we had where it was repeatedly drawn to the attention of the board that the simple statement that a disability had ante-war or post-war causation was not sufficient and was not fair or just to the applicant for a pension. Time and again we get this letter from the pension board: "the claim for disability has not been granted as it is considered of ante-war or post-war causation." We ask that the members of the pension board should go a little further and give their reasons why they consider it ante-war or post-war. The minister of this department and the members of the committee will bear me out in what I say, and yet the same cause of complaint persists. Within the last few months I have had six or seven cases where the board have decided that there was an ante-war or post-war causation. What we are asking is that the board should give their reasons why they consider it ante-war or postwar. None is given. We are therefore in this amendment simply asking that the boot be placed on the other foot, and that instead of the applicant for a pension having to prove his claim it will be up to the board to disprove it. Is there anything unfair or unjust in that? The board have the medical history sheets and the man's whole medical record in their hands; they can command the best medical opinion from one end of this country to the other. Why, then, should it not be easier for the board to disprove the claim of the applicant than for the applicant to prove it to the hilt, as he is now required to do? That is all this motion asks, and I think it is only fair that the board should be asked to disprove the claim rather than the applicant should be called upon to prove it.
Reasons have been given why the board is in a very much better position than tihe applicant to bring forward proof. Let me dilate on a few of them. The board may say: There is nothing in your medical history sheet showing any sickness overseas. That may be so because in the past and right up to the present time we have been legislating against the -man who wanted to carry on in tihe trenches. (Let me repeat that: we have been legislating against the man who wanted to carry on in the trenches, despite his disability. He may have had a slight disability. It may have -come upon -him at a critical moment of the war, and the soldier says to himself: I am not going to desert my comrades. So he goes to tihe regimental aid post and sees the medical officer and gets treatment from him, or maybe he goes back to a rest post for a short
126	COMMONS
War Pensions-Mr. Ross (Kingston)
time. He might just as easily have pressed his disability a little further and have been evacuated to the casualty clearing station or to hospital. Now it was impossible for the regimental medical officer at the aid post to keep records. I appeal to all those who did service, to any medical man in this house or throughout the country who was a regimental medical man. It was impossible for them to keep records. The hon. member for Fort William (/Mr. 'Manion), in his little dugout, had only a little bit of paper on which to note down and send back to the orderly officer of the day the fact that this man had taken treatment from him. He could not keep a medical record book in his little dugout, and unless the man with the disability was evacuated or went to the hospital there would :be little or no record of his sickness. So I say that up to the present we have been legislating against the man who wished to carry on, and who tbore for a time with his disability and his sickness. Then came the time when he was sent home.
I was surprised to hear one member say that we should treat them 'all alike. When these men came back from the war some had been overseas two, three and four years, while others had been over there for only two weeks. There was no difficulty at all for the mau who had been overseas only two weeks not taking his discharge, but the man who had been in the trenches for a year or more was very much disinclined to any further detention for treatment for a disability. If he complained of a disability and the least thing was found wrong with him, he could not go home like his comrades. So I say that in every case we have been making it difficult for the men to have a proper medical record, and I understood that that claim would not 'be put up against the man; that is, that the character of his discharge would not be used against him, but that a decision would be based upon the condition found upon examination at the present time. Surely we are not asking anything unfair when we simply take the boot off the returned soldier's foot and put it on that of the pension board, so that instead of the soldier having to prove his claim to the hilt it will be up t-o the pension board to disprove it. I appeal to anyone in this house if that is unfair. There is nothing unfair or unjust about it. The pension board has everything at its finger's end that is necessary to make out a case. Let me say to the hon. member for Qu'Appelle that we are not seeking to destroy the work of the pension board in any way, but it is up to us to tell the pension board what attitude we 
want them to take towards these cases, and it is up to them to decide whether the man is deserving of a pension or not.
There is another reason why this motion or the amendment should be carried. During the years that pensions have been granted, you have allowed representatives of the pension board to go to the man with a small pension and say to him: My good fellow, you had better commute this .pension. I grant you that that has not been done so much of late, but it was done for many years. Many men who were receiving a five, ten of fifteen per cent pension were told iby the representatives of the board that next year the pension would (be smaller and it would be to the soldier's advantage to commute it and take a lump sum then. There are hundreds of men throughout this country to-day with commuted pensions whose disabilities are returning in an intensified form. What does the board say to them? It says: Before we consider this case you must prove to us that your disability is greater now than it was on the day that you commuted your pension. Now who is in a better position to say whether that disability is greater to-day than the pension board itself? The medical man who attended this applicant may then have been living in Vancouver, and he may now be living in Kingston or Ottawa. How can the soldier go back to the medical man for proof that his disability is greater to-day than it was when he commuted his pension? Who is in a position to say whether that disability is greater to-day? Only the pension board. They have all the medical history sheets and everything connected with the man's case at the time the pension was commuted. All they would then have to do would be to examine the man and take his evidence, and then decide whether or not he should be put back on the pension list. That is a second good reason why this motion or the amendment should pass.
I come to the third reason. Cases have been mentioned to-day of certain disabilities and their possible connection with the war. The pension board have specialists who are advising them whether these disabilities were connected with war service or not, and the advice from these specialists differs in one section from what it is in another, and as a consequence the men are suffering. I say that the pension board should be in a position to disprove any claim if the applicant is not really entitled to a pension.
I hope that I have made myself clear in the three important reasons I have to offer why this motion or the amendment should carry. I believe that this house will consider that it

War Pensions-Mr. Brown
is not an unfair or unjust request to make on behalf of the returned men. The pension board is a strongly fortified unit. It has the evidence at its finger's end and can command the best medical opinions in evidence. It should be an easy matter for them to say whether any man's claim is good or bad. The hon. member for Fort William (Mr. Manion) mentioned yesterday that a man of his former regiment, now living in Kingston, had written to him in regard to his medical record. How can these men locate their officers under whom they served in order to get the necessary evidence to prove their case? It is a most difficult matter for them to undertake.
I do not think we are asking charity for these men; we are simply asking for fairness and justice on their behalf.
We are not unreasonable in asking that the pension board should assume the onus of disproving a man's statement. We are simply asking them to do what they promised to do. They might at least give reasons why they reject a case; but no reason is given beyond the bare notation: ante-war-post war. What is left for the returned man to do? He must go before the federal appeal board, but he goes there without knowing why he has been turned down by the pension board. He is, as it were, disarmed.
I am not so strongly in favour of reinforcing the federal appeal board. I do not think that the federal appeal board has strengthened the returned man's case as many thought it would. The federal appeal board, like any appeal court, can only review the evidence submitted. If one new feature is submitted at the appeal hearing, then the case must go back to the pension board. Undoubtedly if the wish of the members of all parties in this house was carried out in the spirit desired, there would never have been a reason for the federal appeal board being instituted. I am satisfied of that. I do not think we are going to strengthen the case of the returned man or make it one bit better by increasing the number of members of the federal appeal board. We had better get busy and change some of the official representatives who are not doing their duty at the present time in presenting the cases of returned men. I know an instance where the man who should have represented the returned soldier's case before the appeal tribunal, was not in a fit condition to do so. I intend to go further into the case, but I shall first notify the man that I am going to bring it up in this house.
At first I was a little hesitant as to whether we were going far enough with this resolution, but with the amendment I have seconded I believe we have placed the matter in a fair position. I do not think it is unreasonable to ask the board to do things in just a little different way from what they have been doing them. They should give their reasons for determining a case is not proven, instead of dismissing it with the bald notation: ante-war-post-war. For the reasons I have given, Mr. Speaker, I have very much pleasure in supporting the resolution as amended. There are many things to be considered in regard to pensions which we will have plenty of opportunity to discuss later on; but as to the present motion, I think I am in a position to say whether what is proposed would be fair or unfair in view of the wide experience I have had in regard to the wounds, diseases, and other troubles of oui returned men.

Perhaps there is no subject, Mr. Speaker, on which there is more universal agreement in this house than that the present situation in regard to pensions is not satisfactory, and that it is our desire to give every possible consideration to the needs of returned men.
I should be only repeating what has been demonstrated so often if I were- to spend time in pointing out cases in which gross injustice has been done or in which justice has not been done to our returned men. It was very forcibly impressed upon my mind before the war closed, when I saw a young man who had not a scratch on him come back home completely shattered as regards his nerves, that it would be necessary for us to provide special means for dealing with those men who could not prove that their present physical condition was directly attributable to war service. That opinion was abundantly confirmed when on the thirtieth day of January last I went with a young man from my community before the appeal board and found how entirely unsatisfactory the provisions were for dealing with men who could not definitely connect their present physical condition with their war service. No doubt there are hundreds of cases throughout the country where that is so.
It seems to me that the man who in the early stages of the war lost a leg or an arm is not the same object of pity as the man who went through the four years of the hard grind and perhaps never received any external wounds that he could point to as evidence of his service. True, the man who lost a leg or an arm is to be pitied, but I believe that in many cases he is better physically, his morale is better, and he is better morally

I should like m large measure to endorse what was said by the hon. member for London (Mr. White) in regard to such cases as those referred to by the hon. member for Labelle (Mr. Bourassa), that we would not be making any great mistake if we were to consider these men as war casualties. In a very real sense they are war casualties. Many of these men, taken away from surroundings where they were not subjected to such temptations, very readily fell victims to the temptations that confronted them, and, as I have said, I do not think that we would be making any very great mistake if we considered them as war casualties.
Now, I do not intend to discuss this question at any great length. I think we are all agreed that something must be done to give a full measure of justice to the men who served at the front. I was glad to hear the member for Labelle express his sentiments in regard to that matter. Probably on many questions my opinions will differ very widely from his, particularly in regard to Canada's participation in the war; but whatever our views may be on that point, I believe there is a very general opinion that those who did serve in the war should receive the fullest possible measure of justice. But being, as we are, agreed on that question, the question confronting us now is that brought before us by the hon. member for Muskoka (Mr. Mc-Gibbon) in his resolution and in the amendment that has been moved by the hon. member for Queens-Lunemiburg (Mr. Ernst). The hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Speakman) pointed out that the resolution as originally brought before this house practically meant that the Board of Pension Commissioners would simply be a body that would register decisions made by other persons, no matter how reputable those persons might be.
It seems to me, Mr. Speaker, that there is after all very little difference, from a practical point of view, between the original motion and the amendment. I would point out to the mover and seconder of the amendment that there are certain practical considerations which it seems to me they have not taken into account. The hon. member for Lunenburg stated that we were not introducing a new principle, and he cited the analogy, or what he thought was an analogy, of the Customs Act, where men accused of smuggling were required to prove that they had not smuggled

the goods in question. In such a case no hardship is imposed upon the man who is required to prove that certain goods have not been smuggled. In the great majority of cases invoices or bills of lading would be available, or perhaps a sworn statement from the Canadian dealer who had supplied the man with the goods. Those would, in such cases, be readily available. But it is just an instance of how unsafe it is to reason by analogy. Take the other situation that we are asked to consider, where the pension board is required to disprove the man's claim. I admit all the difficulties that have been urged in regard to a man proving his eligibility for pension. I realize the difficulty that confronts him in many cases. I know that the records are incomplete. In the particular case that I took up before the appeal board the other day the records were very incomplete. I recognize all that, but the system as we have it to-day provides that the man shall prove his case to the satisfaction of the pension board. Reverse that position and you say that the pension board must prove that that man has not a good case. Let me ask, prove it to the satisfaction of whom? To the satisfaction of the man?

Mr. Speaker, when the
house rose at six o'clock I was endeavouring to point out what seemed to be an anomaly which would be created if either the original resolution or the amendment were carried by this house. I would be the last person to seek to put any obstacle, however slight, in the way of the fullest possible measure of justice being done to the returned men; I also would be the last to raise any point which might be termed "quibbling". But, Mr. Speaker, when I raised the point that the putting of the onus of disproof on the board would seem to create, at least in my mind, a practical difficulty, I did so because it seemed to me that it would bring about a situation which might possibly create a greater difficulty than the one we are attempting to solve. Possibly, of course, on further reflection I might come to the conclusion that I have been wrong in the way I have looked upon this matter, but that is the way it appears to me at present.
This question of attributability to service always will be a difficult point. It has been a difficult question in the past and the difficulty will become increasingly great as the year.? go by. To prove or disprove a man's eligibility to pension is, in the very nature of the case, impossible with all the exactness of the mathematical demonstration. It simply cannot be done. Suppose, for instance, a man should make application for a pension and that his record showed nothing which would be conclusive either one way or the other. Under the proposal submitted to the house now, that man would come before the pension board and say, "There is a presumption that my claim is good," and there is a good deal to be said for that position. The board, having nothing beyond what appeared in the record on file, would be required to grant him a pension. How would it be possible for the board to give evidence and disprove that man's claim? Would it not be much more practicable for the board to express its sympathy for the man and say to him, "It is true that there is nothing in your record that shows that you are entitled to a pension, but it is possible that you may be able to produce other evidence to which we shall be glad to give consideration."
I mentioned the fact before six o'clock that only a few weeks ago I had accompanied a young man from my own town to present his case to the appeal board. I placed before 2419-9
this young man well before he enlisted for service. He was a strong, vigorous man, accustomed to engage in all kinds of athletic sports. He was accepted as fit; there was no reason to suppose that he was not fit when he was accepted for service, but when he came back from the war it was quite evident to every person who had known him that he had suffered disabilities. There was a hunch on his back; he was by no means the strong, vigorous man he had been. Just here I might add that for a time this young man was given one hundred per cent pension for tuberculosis. Within a month or so afterwards it was decided that he did not have tuberculosis and his pension was withdrawn absolutely, and has been discontinued ever since. The members of the appeal board simply told me that my evidence had no bearing oq the point at all, that it was not worth anything. Would it not be well, when such evidence as that is available-and I think in a great many cases such evidence would be available-to have it accepted by the pension board or the appeal board, whichever body is determining the case? Let the members of the boards be the judges as to the weight of that evidence and the reputation, if you like, of those who present it. Would that not be much better than having the board in the anomalous position they now occupy, that of being judge and litigant at the same time?
That is the way this question appears to me at the moment, Mr. Speaker. While we have the fullest possible sympathy for every returned man, we must try at least to be governed by sound principles in the matter. This is not a question of our unwillingness to assume financial obligations; I have said for years that we have not yet reached the peak of what we will be required to pay for pensions, and I do not believe we will reach that peak for some years to come. I am quite satisfied that the great majority of the people of Canada are willing to assume still further obligations in order that we may do our full duty in this matter, but at the same time, unless we are prepared to throw down the bars and say that every man who enlisted is eligible for pension-and perhaps we may come to that in time-in the meantime it seems to me that we cannot very radically depart from one of the fundamental principles underlying the pension act, and that is that the returned soldier should prove, before a competent



War Pensions-Mr. MacLaren
board, his eligibility for pension. I believe that the act could be framed so that more discretion would be given to the board than they would seem to have at present, enabling them to weigh the evidence and decide what they would accept in coming to their conclusions. There is another valid reason why we should not decide this point at the moment; and that is the giving to the returned men's organizations of the privilege of coming before the committee shortly to be set up and stating their case. I think that will go a long way to meet the claims of the men who have served at the front and who have returned to us crippled and disabled-"burnt-out" seems to be the term most used, and I cannot think of a better one-and unless it can be shown that there is some necessity for departing from the fundamental principles which underlie the act, I think it would be well in the meantime to pause and consider this matter.

Mr. Speaker, the discussion of the past two days has been carried on in such a thorough and excellent manner that I feel I should show my interest and my sympathy with the subject under discussion. It happens that I have been in such intimate contact with disabled soldiers, that I think I should try to add something to the discussion.
The Pension Act is one of evolution and development and is largely dependent upon experience. When it has been found to fail in meeting those cases which it was our desire should be met, then an amendment to the act has been made, but it is still the widespread opinion of the people of the country, and I believe of the members of the house, that the Pension Act as it now stands fails to cover the situation. Up to a certain point it meets the situation satisfactorily, but there are many cases which cannot be dealt with under the provisions of the act as it now stands. Hence the resolution and amendment now before the house. The prolonged war, its intensity and the enormous scale upon which it was carried on, have added unusual features to this question.
As a result of this discussion, I believe the house appreciates the difficulty which the returned soldier has in establishing his case. Quite frequently the record of the soldier fails to show a disability received at the front, especially those of a minor character-the man was returned to duty and no record was made. Then there are many cases where no records exist upon the return of the soldier to Canada. In many cases the men were examined by their physicians but they were

regarded as returned soldiers and were not looked upon as patients in the ordinary sense; they were not charged fees and no record was made of their disabilities. One can well understand that the men did not have the question of pensions in their minds; they did not feel that they would require pensions. Many minor accidents were not appreciated at the time, many diseases were in the early stages and the men were not aware of them. When the development of disease forced these men to take action, they discovered the impossibility of obtaining a record. The medical officers who attended these 'men at the front had scattered all over the country, and in some cases the doctor had died. The same would apply to those doctors consulted upon their return to Canada. One example came under my observation within the last three weeks. This man is now known to have pulmonary tuberculosis. He had written to his doctor asking for a certificate but the answer had come back that he was not remembered. He made that request on several occasions and I suggested to him that he go to see the doctor personally. The doctor lived some considerable distance away, by rail, but when this man visited him he was remembered and was given a certificate. I mention that as an illustration of the difficulties which confront the men in establishing their cases. Many of these men were not so constituted as to have the question of pension in their mind, nor were they thinking of obtaining records or certificates. If that be the case, as I think it unquestionably is, and the country and the house wish cases which can honestly receive pension, to receive it, must we not endeavour to frame the act so that it will meet those cases that have failed to establish or have had great difficulty in establishing their claims?
I would refer to a group of cases which one might call -premature debility or decrepitude. By those I mean men who have had no actual injury or illness but who, after returning, have acquired an early senility or decrepitude over what one could fairly allow for the ten or twelve years since the war. While that may be a difficult task to deal with, on the other hand there are many difficult problems and provision should be made in some w.ay in the act so that as far as possible these premature old men may receive some compensation.
I believe the view in the house and in the country is to widen out the act so as to make it possible for cases to establish their claims which it is thought should be established. This may not be done in a mathematical way.

War Pensions-Mr. Ilsley
If we are looking for precision, exact proof, and ask for it, then we shall pass over many men who in every way have earned pension and should have it. We must be prepared to make it possible for them to establish their hlaims; we must be prepared to accept less rigid and exact evidence, not according to courts of law but according to what seems reasonable under the circumstances. I believe we would then enable the men to obtain justice; we would satisfy the country and we would do away with the complaint which we are constantly hearing, that when the men went overseas they were promised that they would be looked after. I do not blame the legislators in what they have done so far. I believe all the members take a different view to-day from what they did five, six, seven, or eight years ago. It has been a matter of development, of education to us, a truer appreciation of the facts. Therefore I commend the resolution and the amendments to the sympathetic consideration of the house.

I
should like to say a few words on the resolution and the amendment. I was a member of the special parliamentary committee on pensions and returned soldiers' problems in 1928, and I gave these matters some thought at that time. In addition to that, I may say that in the town in Nova Scotia in which I live is a tuberculosis sanatorium and there are found a large number of tubercular returned soldiers who from time to time are applying to the Board of Pension Commissioners for pensions. Very often those men fail to get pensions although they have been suffering from tuberculosis for a number of years. The rule applied by the Board of Pension Commissioners to tuberculosis cases is that unless the applicant showed some sign or symptom of tuberculosis while in the service or within one year after leaving the service, his tuberculosis is not deemed to be attributable to or to have arisen during service. This is a rule adopted by the Board of Pension Commissioners for determining these cases, and I suppose they considered it was about the best practical rule that they could adopt. But the existence of the rule creates some dissatisfaction, for the very reason that has been emphasized by so many speakers during the debate. Frequently the men cannot give evidence of having consulted a physician within the first twelve months after their discharge, though often they are in a position to give evidence of having consulted a physician shortly after the expiration of that, period. That is simply one class, and, I think, a fairly large class, of cases which 2419-9J
seems to call for some amendment to the Pension Act. There are, of course, not only cases of tuberculosis, but cases of heart trouble and these "burnt-out" cases which seem in many instances incapable of definite diagnosis. I think the opinion so widely expressed in this debate, that there should be some radical amendment to the Pension Act, is the opinion that one finds throughout the country as a whole.
The whole question is what amendment either to the act or to the regulations is the best one. We have before the house for its consideration the resolution proposed by the hon. member for Muskoka-Ontario (Mr. Mc-Gibbon) who was a member of the committee of 1928. This afternoon the hon. member for Queens-Lunenburg (Mr. Ernst) proposed an amendment which differs from the resolution in two or three respects. In the first place, by the resolution the only persons affected were those who suffered in a theatre of war. The amendment, however, applies to everyone who was in the service. In the second place, by the resolution, the opinion of a medical man was a prerequisite to the shifting of the onus of proof, -but by -the amendment moved this afternoon there is no such prerequisite. I have given some thought to the amendment and to the resolution and it occurs to me that possibly neither will reach the class of cases that most of the members desire to meet. If w-e throw upon the Board of Pension Commissioners the onus of disproving any claim that may be made for a pension where disability exists, I suppose it follows that we shall have to add very considerably to the powers of the Board of Pension Commissioners, that is to say, we shall have to give the Board of Pension Commissioners power to question the applicant, to question the doctors who have been treating the applicant during the past few years, and perhaps in other ways to compel persons to give evidence. I think that follows, otherwise an applicant might simply come before the Board of Pension Commissioners, prove his disability, and -then, by being silent, legally compel the board to grant him a pension. I think if hon. members of the house will consider the amendment, they will see that that is its result. I fancy that there would be no objection on the part of any member -to increasing the powers of the board in that respect. They will have to have power to make investigation because the onus of disproof is thrown upon them, and if we throw the onus of disproof upon them, we must give them some power of disproof. I can see that if the board assumes the duty of

It may be suggested that that is not the right way to deal with this class of cases at all, and I have heard it suggested that in a certain class of cases the principle of attributability, which is the principle underlying the act at the present time, will have to be discarded, so that the very existence of disability coupled with military service will entitle men to a pension without making it necessary for any tribunal to decide whether it is attributable to war service or not. All these facts simply show this, that the proper way to deal with this particular class of cases which everyone wants to deal with properly, is to have the parliamentary committee which is to be appointed this year bring before them the representatives of the returned soldier organizations. I also think that it would be necessary for us to discuss the matter with the Board of Pension 'Commissioners and with the federal appeal board, If we approach the matter in that way, I think we shall be able to arrive at a very much better solution so far as the interests of the returned soldiers are concerned than we can reach by debating a resolution of this kind. The method that has been followed in previous years has been the right method, the method of dealing with these matters by a special parliamentary committee. It is an effective method, a frank and searching method. My attitude towards this resolution and the amendment, unless something comes out of the debate that I do not anticipate at the moment, is that this matter should go to the parliamentary committee which is to be appointed to consider this and other returned soldier problems.
Mr. .TAMES ARTHURS (Parry Sound): During all the years that the Pension Act has been in force and the question of pensions has become a live one, there has been one bugbear continually before the eyes of the
framers of the act and of those who were endeavouring to make it more effective. This bugbear arose from a knowledge of the experience of the republic to the south of us after the civil war with respect to so-called abuses of the pension acts adopted by that country. Since the war we have had various amendments to the Pension Act. In the early stages these amendments had largely to do with the class of men who could become pensioners or with the amount of pension to be granted to them. Latterly other difficulties have arisen, and during the last two or three years the question before the public in regard to the returned man has been that which has been so frequently referred to to-day, the question whether or not a disability was incurred during the war, previous to the war, or subsequent to the man's return to civil life. Personally I believe that where a man has a disability and has served in the actual theatre of war, the pension board should not be permitted to set up the plea that it was a prewar disability. If the man was fit enough to go out and fight in the actual theatre of war it should be taken for granted that he was in sufficiently good health to enable him to carry on.
The other question is a good deal more difficult. A great deal has been said in the course of this debate regarding the man who came back, went to work and tried to earn a living, making the best of his health condition as he found it. As has 'been pointed out, many of our young men were discharged as A-l who were really suffering disability, some from wounds, some from disease. I know a young man nineteen years of age who was discharged as A-l only a few weeks after having received gunshot wounds in the lung. In that case I had great difficulty in getting this young man vocational training. He was totally unfit to go back on the farm. These cases occur from time to time. I might illustrate their nature by a case (that I have under my attention at the present time. A young man, a member of the first Canadian contingent, was wounded and gassed on the occasion when the Germans first put over gas at Ypres; he was kept in a German prison and returned to Canada at the conclusion of the war. His lung condition was not good then and has never been good since. He was pensioned at twenty per cent disability for bronchial trouble. At his own request and the request of his friends this young man has been repeatedly sent up for medical examination and requests have been made to the Board of Pension Commissioners that he should be granted' full pension. On every
War Pensions-Mr. Hoicden

occasion the reply of the board has 'been in about three words: mo further pensionable disability. They give no reason whatever for rids decision. When this young man came lome at ithe conclusion of the war he.set up \. little business for himself driving a taxi cab. 3ut gradually he has failed in health. Every->ody in ithe small town where this young iellow lives knows that he got gradually worse ind worse until he was not able to earn a dollar ait all and that during the last three or four years he has been supported by charity.
This brings up another question, Mr. Speaker: who should 'take oare of these men? Our charitable institutions are taxed to the limit at the present time, and very rightly they object to taking care of a case of this kind where ithe man is manifestly entitled to compensation for ill health that, to a layman, is clearly and obviously the result of military service.
I believe the proper course to enable the pension board to deal with these oases is somewhat along the lines suggested by this resolution. I am not particular as to the wording of the resolution; it is results we want to get. Something should be done to help out these men.
The member for Lisgar (Mr. Brown) who so far as I have observed voiced the only objection to 'this resolution, admitted that in many cases there was nothing on the file of the soldier to show any reason for his disability; consequently the board would be unable to disprove the man's allegation that he was suffering from disability incurred' during the war. But I would point out to the hon. member and to others who think with him that if it is. difficult or well nigh impossible for the board to disprove the man's allegation, how much more difficult it must be for the man himself who during the intervening years since the end of the war has in many cases been trying to carry on on hiis own without any pension. Mr. Speaker, as a civilian doctor I should like to say a word or two on this resolution. According to its terms the onus shall be placed on the Board of Pension Commissioners, first, to disprove illness in any given case, and secondly to disprove that such illness was attributable to overseas service. Without very much effort I can think of half a dozen cases of returned men who have come to my office

and who were discharged from the army apparently in perfect condition; to-day they are helpless wrecks. They are receiving no disability pension, and it is a shame and a disgrace to this country. That these cases do exist is beyond question; there are very many of them.
There is another class of cases. I know' a man who enlisted and served with the army throughout the course of the war. He was not overseas, and he was discharged in fairly good condition, but to-day he also is a helpless invalid and gasping for breath most of the time. I maintain that this man also, although he was not out of Canada, should be considered eligible to receive a pension. I am glad to say that after some considerable trouble this man was given a fairly substantial pension.
There is still another class of cases, of which I will name an example. A man of mature age, the father of a grown family, who for at least ten years before the outbreak of the war suffered from a chronic condition, enlisted in the city of Winnipeg and was sent overseas. He spent two years overseas, I think probably the best two years of his life up to that time. Since his return to Canada he has been on a pension and he has spent a good deal of his time in the hospital. I believe quite honestly and candidly that the war never did him anything but good in one way and another, because he certainly was not in the actual field of war.
' There is, sir, still another class of cases that medical men have to deal with from time to time. They come to the office and they complain of many things, loss of appetite, sleeplessness, weakness, inability to earn a living and what not, and yet when subjected to a fairly rigid examination one fails-at least I have failed on many occasions-to find any cause to which their symptoms could be attributable. I do not wish to say that these men are not sick. I certainly would be the last one to wish to see them unfairly treated, but the fact remains that to the best of my ability I have been unable to find any cause for such symptoms. Any person who has been overseas, in my estimation, should receive the most careful and sympathetic consideration of the country in respect to any breakdown, whether premature or otherwise, that occurs after his return to Canada, and I will even go so far as to say that such a person should receive a pension even if his disability were not due to overseas service. But I think this country needs to be very careful of a certain class, that is, those individuals who are probably

War Pensions-Mr. Cantley
not sick except in their own minds, and undoubtedly a fair proportion of such men appeal to medical men for certificates stating that they are suffering from one disease or another. Having in mind, as I said before, that it is necessary for the Board of Pension Commissioners to disprove the illness, and considering that, in the second place, they must prove that such illness is not attributable to overseas service, I would like to say. sir. that there is no doctor or body of doctors in the country who can say after ten years that, to begin with, the man is not suffering, if he says he is from a certain illness, and. as well, who are able to disprove that such illness is attributable to the war. It is a very big question. If a man comes to a doctor's office and says he is sick, the doctor may say: "I cannot find anything the matter with you," and when he cannot say that then I believe the Board of Pension Commissioners is in just such a position. Therefore if this resolution were adopted in toto by this house I think it would be exposing the Dominion of Canada to very heavy pension payments, because I do not believe that the Board of Pension Commissioners would be able to disprove such claims on the part of applicants as is stated here. For this reason, sir, I think that such matters require careful consideration, and should be decided only after mature consideration on the advice of eminent specialists in medicine and surgery. I am therefore not entirely in favour of the motion.

Mr. Speaker, I wish to thank the members for Muskoka-Ontario (Mr. McGibbon), the mover of this resolution, and the member for Queens-Lunenburg (Mr. Ernst), the mover of the amendment, for bringing this matter before the house. We have prided ourselves a good deal on the generous way in which we have treated our returned men. Canada has pensioned about 161,000 cases out of some 215,000 casualties. I would point out that the United States has pensioned over three times that number, with a total list of casualties considerably less than those of our troops who served in the great war. Personally I have no fault to find with the Board of Pension Commissioners in so far as my dealings with them are concerned on behalf of quite a number of my constituents who have had cases before that board. My trouble is not with the Board of Pension Commissioners but with the regulations under which they act and which, in my judgment, have been much too narrow and restricted. We must
not forget that practically all the men who lived in France and Flanders during those horrible years worked under what, to use an engineering term, might be called forced draft, that is, they worked not under ordinary conditions but under wholly abnormal and high pressure conditions; they lived as long in twenty-four hours as most of us now do in a month, with corresponding wear and tear on their nerves and every other vital force of which they were possessed. The result of that is evident now in many cases. I know it will be said that men in 1919 took thew discharge claiming that they were physically fit and under no disability resulting from their war service when they themselves then knew such was not the case. In 1919 I saw scores of our men, and many from my own county, in some of the hospitals in London and elsewhere, whose only desire at that time was to get home. Later they reached Halifax within one hundred miles of their homes in the county of Pictou. Many of them, so far as they possibly could, waived or evaded the medical examination, and many of them, I have no doubt, knowingly made statements in regard to their condition which were not strictly true. Why? Simply because they wanted to get home. They were within a few miles of home and their great desire was to get there. Can you blame them? I certainly do not, and it should not be held against them to-day when they find that they are not in the condition they thought they were in at the time of demobilization.
Some reference has been made to-day in this house to the powers given to a collector of national revenue. I put it to you, sir, and I put it to the house, are not our returned men entitled to equal protection with the collectors of revenue of this country? That is putting it on pretty low ground, but these men are not to-day receiving equal treatment with the collectors of the revenue of Canada.
I would like to congratulate the member for London (Mr. White) on his courage and his fairness in regard to such of the men as were overseas who were doubly unfortunate. WTith his views I am in complete agreement. And with regard to the member for Lisgar (Mr. Brown), with whom I seldom find myself in agreement, I am glad to know that in this case he takes more the attitude of the Good Samaritan than he does of the high priest, or rather the priest referred to in the parable.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have pleasure indeed in joining with my hon. friend from Pictou (Mr. Cantley) in offering congratulations to the hon. member for Muskoka-Ontario (Mr. Mc-Gibbon.) and my hon. friend from Queems-Lunenburg (Mr. Ernst) in the resolution and amendment they have placed before this house. As we have been told by several hon. gentlemen, this is perhaps one of the most important subjects to come before this house for many sessions. It is a fact that in considering this problem we are dealing with a great section of our population, perhaps the most important section of this great Dominion ; I refer to the men who left this country years ago, unsolicited in most cases, to the number of over 500,000; who went to foreign shores to fight for what they believed and what we all believed to be the side of justice and right.
We all know and can hardly forget the promises which were made to those men before they left Canada. Why, sir, from every platform in this country; from every school-house; from every pulpit; at every outdoor meeting in the days of 1914 and the few years immediately succeeding, every man and woman who said a word in advocacy of the cause of freedom made it plain indeed that the boy who went forth in defence of his country could expect from Canada -when he came back, everything that it was possible for his country to give. With that promise, more than 500,000 of our sons left this country and did noble duty in foreign fields. When these boys were asked to go over the tap and bare their breasts to the German bayonets, they did not think of the days to come; they thought only of Canada, their home; they thought only of the fight they were there to make for this country in order to

see that Canada continued to exist. That being so, I believe to-day it is our duty to see that these boys receive everything that is coming to them, and a little more.
It has been said that many thousands of our boys were discharged as A-l when that should not have been done. We must remember that these boys had been over there for two, three or four years and were very anxious to get home. Whether they had been ill or disabled they were so anxious to get home that in many cases they would not appear before the board, with the result that many who should not have been discharged as being in good health came back discharged as A-l. I am sorry that such was the case; some advice should have been given to these men as to the possible result of such action. Nevertheless, they came back. Now we have a pension board, and no matter what may be said against that board, in my opinion, it is composed of honest -men who are anxious to do what is right and who are sympathetic indeed to the ex-soldiers. However, the members of this board are bound by a law which prevents them from doing full justice to the men who served overseas. The same thing applies to the Minister of Pensions and National Health (Mr. King, Kootenay). I have found him most sympathetic indeed in connection with the few cases which it has been my privilege to bring before him, but he also is bound down; he can go so far and no further. I have in mind two or three cases from my own county. One case was that of a man who, while serving in this country as a military police officer, contracted cold and developed tonsilitis. From that, as very often follows, he developed rheumatism and eventually a very serious heart affection. That man was discharged. When he had these slight tonsil affections he was not really sick enough to see a physician and the result was that he passed along and had no medical examination, so when the time came for his application for pension to be considered he had no medical proof to offer that he had suffered from tonsilitis 'while on service. As I said, he eventually developed a very serious heart condition. A year or so ago that same man, almost a hopeless invalid, appealed to me to help him, having tried many times, but without success, to secure a favourable verdict from the Board of Pension Commissioners. Unfortunately he could not offer evidence that he had been ill during his period of service, although I am absolutely sure that his statement was quite true. Within the last two months this man made a great struggle to come to Ottawa and appear before

War Pensions-Mr. Spankie
the board personally, without an invitation and without any right or reason; he exerted himself to such an extent that to-day he is under the sod. There was a man who was entitled to a pension if ever a soldier from Canada was entitled to one, yet he is gone without having received any recognition at all, leaving a wife and four or five children practically homeless and without means of support.
Cases of that character come under our notice rather too frequently. Take the cases of those whom we call "lungers," men who to-day are suffering from some weakness of the lungs, from tuberculosis or something of that kind. Many of these men to-day are invalids simply because of the fact that they served in France, and while that condition may not have developed at the time, it was undoubtedly brought about by their service and their exposure while overseas. I will say for the minister that in one or two cases which I brought before him he showed great sympathy indeed, but unfortunately because of the pension act which is in force in this country to-day he was unable to do more than give these men perhaps two or three months' treatment in a hospital. _
I say this to the Minister of Pensions and National Health, Mr. Speaker: any man who develops a lung condition, whether or not that condition can be directly attributed to his war service, should receive hospitalization treatment, because tuberculosis can be cured if these cases are treated in time and in a proper way. I believe the minister should be given power to give these men the proper treatment.
It has been said here that the resolution of the hon. member for Muskoka-Ontario goes too far -because this question is being left in the hands of the doctors. Doctors may or may not be honest, but I 'have been one for several years and I ha-ve yet to find a dishonest medical man. If hon. members of this house and the people of Canada feel that the doctors cannot be trusted in cases of this kind, I would ask that it be remembered that the very lives of many of our citizens are placed in the hands of our judges. Do we find fault with them? Surely the doctors of Canada are as hounourable as the judges, and no man would ever say a word against the honour of those learned -gentlemen.
For these reasons, Mr. -Speaker, I have much pleasure indeed in supporting the amendment to the resolution of the hon. member for Queens-iLunenburg. I would like to go mu-ch farther than the amendment -proposes, but in the absence of anything stronger I am quite satisfied to support the amendment.

Let us enact legislation which will be a credit to this parliament and which will cause the name of this country to live long in history.
In common with other members of this house, I have received many applications from returned men for pensions or -increases in pensions. I investigated personally some of these cases an-d I found the facts as stated to be correct. One of these cases is now in the civic hospital in this city. this case, as I have received nothing but courteous treatment from the members of the Board of Pension Commissioners. I want to join with other hon. mem-

bers in saying that I feel exceedingly sympathetic toward the men who were in ithe war for either a long or a slhort period. Attributability is a hard thing to prove, and we should so amend the law that if attributability cannot be proved, at least the benefit of the doubt or a portion of it will go to the soldier. I have cases, as have all of us, where soldiers are totally disabled and yet where we are not able to secure pensions for them. I cannot understand why the onus of proof should rest upon the sick and discouraged man. He is possibly poor; he lives distant from any centre where he could get help to prepare a case; he does not quite know how ito go about the matter and I do not think the onus of proof should be upon him.
I was not in the house all afternoon, so I cannot say just where I stand in regard to the different resolutions and amendments that have been offered, but I hope we can inject some more humanity into the present law or, if we cannot do that, amend ic in the interests of the men who fought the war. I do not take very seriously the argument that it will cost Canada a great deal, because if Canada wants war, she must pay for it. Surely we should not ask these men who fought the war to suffer financially as well as physically and mentally. They have suffered; they are suffering physically and mentally, and we who did not suffer as -they did are the ones who should pay in order that they may live in comparative safety and comfort so far as the security of their families is concerned'.
I have in the riding of Southeast Grey two cases which I suppose are typical, and I will cite them briefly. One is the case of a man who was a minister but who was a private in the ranks. He was shell-shocked, but feeling that other oases were much more serious than his, he did not. report to the hospital and carried on. That man to-day is a complete wreck, able to do no work at all. He did not apply for pension within the time set by the law. He did not want to ask the country to bear any expense for him. He tried to carry on as a minister and moved out of the province of Ontario into the province of Nova Scotia. He has quite a sized family and now we cannot even get a mother's pension for that family because they have been out of the province for a period of seven years.

War Pensions-Mr. Stewart (Leeds)
The other is a medical doctor from the same village. This man went overseas. He was in an ambulance corps close up to the front until he went completely to pieces and was sent to a nerve hospital in Great Britain. He remained there until the end of the war; he was taken home in a 'hospital dhip; he was put into a hospital in Toronto and he was discharged as an A-l man. He is trying to carry on a general practice but he cannot do it. He is working a few days and in bed a few, and he sometimes closes his office for a month at a time. The Tesult is that his practice is going to pieces. He is not able to work in any other way and his family suffer.
I feel that these two cases are only typical of many others and I think the members of the commons this year, if we do nothing else -and if we are to judge from the speech from the throne, we dhall not do much else-should at least see to it that we do something for the returned soldiers and that we do not ask these men to bear the misery and agony of not knowing where the meals are to come from for their Children, of seeing their children grow up without the education that the ordinary people are able to give to theirs. I think some person said that this question should be taken out of party politics. I agree; and so should all other questions.

speechtext:
From
time to time in the course of our discussions there are presented for consideration subjects which have a local application, but the subject which we are discussing to-day is one which is truly national in its character. It is one which has the same application to all parts of the Dominion. It is one in connection with which the experiences of all boh. members are practically identical. That is disclosed bs- the discussions which have taken place in the house to-day, and in discussing this resolution and the amendment that has been moved to it, I feel that we are dealing with a subject of first-olass importance, one that over and above all others deserves our serious consideration and action at the earliest possible moment.
The principle underlying the present Pension Act is, as 1 understand it, that in order that the returned soldier may receive compensation for disability, the onus of proof is on him to show that the disability was incurred during service or aggravated by service or attributable to service. When he attempts to prove that, he is confronted with the record of his service. It appears to me from my experience that the pension board is disposed to pay too much attention to this record and to hold the applicant altogether too strictly to it, a record which is undoubtedly in many instances imperfect, a record which must be imperfect when we consider the circumstances under which it was made, where it was made, when it was made, how it was made, and by whom it was made. He brings the best evidence that he can procure in support of his case and, having done this, he fails to convince the pension board that he is entitled to a pension. He then considers what should be done and he may be advised to carry his case before the appeal board. If he docs this, he finds that the appeal board is rather hampered and restricted in its jurisdiction. He cannot adduce before that board any new evidence, and he must rely upon the evidence which he has adduced before the Board of Pension Commissioners and upon which his application has been rejected. I suggest that the appeal board have authority to receive any new evidence the applicant may be able to submit in support of his case. It is useless circumlocution to send the applicant back to the pension board with this new evidence to await their decision, and, if dissatisfied with that decision, to come before the appeal board again on this new evidence. The difficulty arises in connection with a number of cases which are perhaps on the border line, cases that have been discussed fully and intelligently by the medical men of this house. We have all had experience of such cases.
I submit that the pension board would be entitled to draw inferences from certain facts which are undoubtedly in the record in some cases, and which are proven by other evidence. Our courts draw inferences every day from certain facts which are proven, and which they say should lead irresistibly to certain conclusions. Again we often arrive at a conclusion in very serious cases on circumstantial evidence only. Men have lost their lives, have been executed by the state, when the only evidence against them was circumstantial and in face of their positive denial of any guilt whatever. As I understand the practice of the pension board, they are not inclined to give to circumstantial evidence that weight which the courts give to it, and which I submit the board should give to it. Sometimes, too, in arriving at a conclusion we are forced to adopt a process of rejection. Let us examine every theory that can possibly account for the returned man's condition. Examine his family history, ascertain his condition when he entered the service, trace all these matters
HO	COMMONS
War Pensions-Mr. Johnstone (Cape Breton)
up, and then if we are unable to find therein anything that should force us to the conclusion that his condition is due to disease in the natural course, let'us give him the benefit of the doubt and presume that his condition is due to war service. In the practice of the law we have presumptions; we have rebuttable presumptions and irrebuttable presumptions. The object and purpose of this resolution and of the amendment is to set up in favour of the disabled man a presumption. We do not go so far as to contend that this presumption is absolutely irrebuttable, but what we say is that it is a presumption, and that until that presumption is rebutted it shall stand in his favour. Surely the Board of Pension Commissioners, with all the machinery at their command, with all their experts and all the records which are open to them, should be able in cases where it would be unfair and improper to accept this presumption, to rebut it without taking a position of antagonism to the soldier, or being compelled, as it were, to be one of the litigants. To a certain extent they are in that position now, because when a returned soldier applies for a pension they apply certain tests. They have experts who examine him with a view to testing the accuracy of his story and ascertaining his true condition, and they exercise their judgment upon the facts ascertained. So we are not asking them to do anything more perhaps than they are actually doing now.
_ The amendment I think places the matter in a better position than the resolution in the first instance. It is to be wondered at, Mr. Speaker, that, with the accumulation of these cases that must have been brought to the attention of the Minister of Pensions, he has not introduced long before this some amendment to meet this type of cases. Practically all members of the house have brought to his attention cases of extreme hardship, cases in which they are absolutely convinced of the honesty of the applicant, but notwithstanding their best endeavours they have failed to make any progress because of the presumption that is against the soldier, because of the onus that is cast upon him. It is unfortunate, I say, that the Minister of Pensions has, as it were, left himself to be driven by the force of public opinion outside this house and by this resolution to take some action in this matter.
I sincerely hope that the amendment as proposed will be given effect to. It can be safeguarded. It only creates a presumption, and not an irrebuttable presumption, and it will do justice, I am sure, in a large number of cases of extreme hardship which have been awaiting the consideration of the department, and in which too often there has been al-
together too long a delay. I propose to support the resolution, and I trust that it will meet with the approval of the house.

speakeroldname: Mr. L. W. JOHNSTONE (Cape Breton North-Victoria):
subtopic: DISABILITIES DUE TO WAR SERVICE-ONUS OP DISPROOF ON PENSION BOARD
speechtext:
I should like to associate
myself with the mover of the resolution (Mr. McGibbon). The question that is before the house is one of the most important that has come before parliament since I have sat here during the last four years. It affects a large portion of the population of Canada and a class of people whom we might term as the saviours of our country, who in defence of our country have become, some of them, permanently disabled, while others are suffering serious disabilities. We have not as a government in any way rewarded the soldiers who have come back. Some blame the pension board; others lay the blame elsewhere. For my part I have been before the pension board with cases on a great many occasions, and I must say that I have always been treated by them with the greatest courtesy and consideration. Whenever it was not possible for them to grant the application I supported, there was always some good reason given for it. It seems to me the reason is that the power of the pension board is limited, and I think the resolution as amended, if implemented by legislation, would help the board considerably. They would be able to go further then they are doing at present, feeling that they have the people of Canada behind them.
Also, I think it would be a good thing for the pension board to travel more across the country. As a colliery doctor I have had a good deal of experience in dealing with cases of returned men and have experienced considerable trouble in getting their medical history. Colliery doctors do not always keep an exact record of their visits. Quite a number of our men who were discharged as A-l, due to their anxiety to get home, after resuming work for a short time have had to give up owing to ill health. To-day I have numerous cases of men suffering from tuberculosis, bronchitis, heart disease and other troubles which, as medical men know, are caused by gassing and other hardships incident to war service. It is very difficult for any doctor to give a complete medical history of such men. For instance, a man comes to you complaining that he has been ailing for some time; he tells you he came out of the war apparently well, but subsequently developed symptoms of lung or heart disease; you question him and find he was gassed overseas or went through a severe nervous

War Pensions-Mr. Robinson
strain which has affected his nervous system. That man applies to the Board of Pension Commissioners for a pension, he goes to Halifax, and the pension authorities there send the papers to the man's doctor to furnish information as to whether the heart or lung affection took place after the war or was present before the war. As I say, it is very difficult for a doctor to give that information; you do not remember whether you attended the man before the war, and you cannot give the board any history of his illness at the time, nor can you say that he contracted it during the war. You can only treat the man as you see him after the war. In many instances such a pension application is rejected, and I am still working on many cases of this kind. On the other hand there are men getting pensions who are not so well entitled to receive them as are others who are not getting anything.
I agree with one of the hon. members who said to-night that any man who went to the war should be rewarded in some way. When we think of the great results accomplished we should be ready and willing to grant a reward to out returned men for all they did for us.
Only to-day I received a letter from a doctor in the United States telling me of a young man whom he has been treating for a year or two. The doctor says:
His arm greatly handicaips him in his work. There is shrapnel embedded in the upper arm, which causes suppuration frequently, totally incapacitating him from work for periods of two to four weeks. He has had the opinions of some of the best surgeons in England, where he spent several months in the ai'my hospital, and also in this country, particularly in the Veterans hospital in Philadelphia. The consensus of opinion is that the shrapnel cannot be removed with safety, and that the result would be worse than the present condition due to nerve injuries that would be involved.
This condition is gradually undermining his health and he is not in as good shape as he was a year ago. This has made it impossible for him to continue his work as chemist and necessary for him to seek work that will take him out of the fumes and air of the laboratory into the out-of-doors. This work will be less remunerative for a considerable time at least, even if he should be able to keep at it continuously, which my past knowledge leads me to say with certainty that he will not.
That man has a mother whom he is trying to assist. He is getting a pension of thirty dollars a month, and he is asking for fifty dollars, which I do not think is too much to allow him. That is one case; like other medical men I could quote hundreds of such cases. I do think that this resolution as amended should be accepted by the government and implemented by the necessary legislation. Personally I am pleased to support it.

subtopic: DISABILITIES DUE TO WAR SERVICE-ONUS OP DISPROOF ON PENSION BOARD
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am delighted to congratulate the mover of this resolution (Mr. McGibbon), and also the mover of the amendment thereto (Mr. Ernst). Coming from the border cities on the Detroit river where we have thousands and thousands of returned soldiers, a large number of whom live across the river, I am in contact nearly every day with these cases, and some of them are very distressing. I have in mind the case of a railroad man who is suffering from epileptic fits. He refrained from putting in an application for pension for years as it would have meant the loss of his position as switchman on the railway, for which he had to be one hundred per cent perfect. Now he is unable to find employment of any kind. At the front he was wounded in the head, and, as I said, he is now subject to epileptic fits. A good many of these cases are outlawed owing to the fact that it is impossible to get an unbroken medical history, especially from men who while they were able to work would not apply for a pension.
Later on we shall have to take into consideration the establishment of homes for old soldiers. Many of them are reaching that stage where they have no parents or other relatives to look after them. At present I have a resolution from the Canadian Legion, Windsor, to be presented at the proper time, asking the department to take this into consideration.
Another distressing case I recall was that of a man with a wife and five children. He was totally incapacitated in consequence of war service, but the poor fellow's application for pension was rejected. He appealed, but became so discouraged that before his appeal was dealt with he committed suicide, feeling assured that his wife would receive a widow's allowance as well as an allowance for the children. Four days afterwards word was received that his appeal had been allowed and a pension granted. I have heard of three or four other similar cases. Some of the cases cited this afternoon were very distressing. The pension board will not tell the wife the reason why her husband is not eligible for a pension, and rightly so, and naturally she thinks it a great hardship that her husband is not treated fairly when she sees other returned men getting pensions who probably were not over at the front any longer than her husband.
To-day our industries insist on maximum efficiency, and they will not take on men over forty or forty-five years of age. This is a great hardship to many of our old soldiers. It means that not only will there be a demand for old age pensions at an earlier age, but

War Pensions-Mr. Plunkett
more soldiers will need to be taken care of in this way. Many men have told me that they feel like broken down race horses; that they cannot work for long without quitting to take a rest-that is, so many hours a day or two or three days a week; that is all they can stand. A good many of these men have continued so far without even applying for pension. I think they are to be congratulated; they should receive some consideration when they will not apply for pension until in duty bound to themselves and to those dependent upon them they feel they must do so. I hope that this resolution will carry unanimously. I feel sure from the sentiments expressed in the house that no hon. member regards it as a political question, and it will certainly open the door to a lot of deserving cases.

subtopic: DISABILITIES DUE TO WAR SERVICE-ONUS OP DISPROOF ON PENSION BOARD
speechtext:
No proposal, Mr. Speaker, which could come before this house would be calculated to create so much interest and have such an important bearing upon the well-being of the citizens of this country as the resolution and amende ment now under consideration. They affect the citizens in many ways. They affect the returned men and their employers. It is to the employers of this country that the government looks for taxes to carry on its system of government. In many instances in Canada business men are trying to employ returned men, but they find it impossible, owing to their physical condition, to keep them in steady employment. It seems to be one of the fatal results of the war that a returned man who makes an effort to work finds that his strength will not permit him to do so; he can work possibly part of the time, but he cannot work all the time. Taking these things into consideration, should we not make the pension board and the appeal board easier of access, the approach to them more reasonable? In talking with many of the returned men, I find they seem to feel that they almost have to gird on as much armour to go before the appeal board or the pensions board as they did in France. That does not seem to me to be the way the people of Canada expected to treat the men when they came home. What is happening to-day in many of our cities? The women of this country, through their societies and auxiliaries, are still taking care of many of the returned men. They are endeavouring to give them the comforts which the government and we, the members of this House of Commons, should legislate to see that they get. I do not blame the pension board; I hold the hon. members of this house responsible. We are the ones who make the laws, and if the pension board do not suit us we should change the law with respect to the

pension board so that comfort- may be brought to the returned men. It was not long ago hat we spoke of our duty as members. There :s not a member in the house who does not say that this is not a political issue. Why, then, do we not adopt this amendment and make it evident to the pension board and to the committee to be appointed by this house that they have our entire sympathy in enlarging this law? That is all that it is necessary for us to do. Not along ago, I believe it was in 1927, a resolution dealing with this matter was brought forward in the house and perhaps it would have been better had we adopted that resolution. Let us not make another mistake such as that. And are we doing our duty in another way? Let me quote from those lines so familiar to all of us-In Flanders' Fields:
To you from failing hands we throw the torch;
Be yours to hold it high.
Hon. members of this house, that applies to us. Are we holding the torch high to-day when we permit the women of this country in all the different cities throughout Canada to put on tag days and sell poppies to bring comfort to our returned men? Is that holding high the torch? That should apply to us just as surely as to all the citizens of our Dominion; for it was written for all.
I am in favour of the amendment.. I hope and trust that hon. members of this house will take such action as will give the lead to the committee which they appoint so that they will know that it is our desire to be generous toward the returned men of this country.
