speechtext:
It must, be a great source of satisfaction to see the unanimity displayed by all parties in this house in respect to their attitude towards the returned soldier. For my own part I hake a very keen interest in the returned soldier question, because I come from a county that had the unique experience of having recruiting stopped, one of the few counties, I suppose, in the whole Dominion of Canada where the recruiting officers had to be taken away in order that enough people should be left in the county to work the mines. When the war came there was one class of people in this country that responded as a man to the call of arms, and they were the miners. From the county of Cape Breton they enrolled as fast as offioers could take their names, until at last the thing became so serious that, as I say, recruiting had to be stopped. Unfortunately the miners were peculiarly susceptible to injuries that prevented them from carrying on their regular work. I have had .many cases of returned

I Tar Pensions-Mr. MacDonald (Cape Breton)
men, miners, who oonitraohed some sort of pulmonary trouble that disabled them from working in the mines. I suppose that I have had before the pension board as many applications as, if not more than, any other hon. member in the house. I must say that the pension hoard have always received those applications with consideration, but they found that theiir hands were tied and with very many deserving cases they could do nothing. One thing I am convinced of, Mr. Speaker, is that the pension board is entirely too email to do the work. The pension board should consist of at least nine or ten members, and it would be very well indeed in the reorganization of the board to adopt the suggestion of the hon. member for Burrard (Mr. Clark), and have the pension board do the travelling with the appeal board sitting in Ottawa. I have in my county some three branches of the legion, and each one of those branches has a number of cases to look after on account of some defect in the Pension Act, because the miners are unable to get their pensions.
The miner returned to Canada and, like many others, he was anxious to reach his home with the least possible delay. Perhaps he had some throat trouble which did not seem serious at the time, but he found after working in the mines for a short period that the trouble had accelerated, that the gas had left its effects on him and that he had to discontinue his work. I have one case in particular now pending before the hoard, the case of a young man who was eighteen years of age at the time of .the war, the picture of health, and strong physically. He was not allowed to enlist in Cape Breton. He stole away to Halifax and enlisted, went through the war, and was wounded and gassed in France. Upon his return he tried to go to work and in fact succeeded in working for a few months.' Since then he has been working intermittently, but has been unable to get any pension and to-day finds it impossible to earn a living.
I must say that at first I had some doubt as to whether this resolution or the amendment would meet the difficulties we have all experienced. It simply shifts the onus from the man to the board, but unfortunately the board as at present constituted is the judge as to whether or not the attributafoility to service has been disproved. That was the difficulty which presented itself to me. It has been suggested that a new organization will have to be set up, perhaps a king's proctor or something of that sort, in order that a thorough examination may be made as to the truth of the statements of all applicants. However that may be, there is one fundamental principle we must remember; it is that a man who served three, four or five years overseas did not return in as good condition as he went away. As other hon. members have pointed out, the trouble may not be apparent at the time; it may develop later, when it may be almost impossible to present a legal continuity of proof tracing that disability to his service overseas. However, while the resolution and amendment are nof perfect and probably will require further improvements by the committee or in some other way, I believe this is a step in the direction of removing a great many of the difficulties which now confront the ex-service men, and I shall have very much pleasure in supporting the proposal.

SMITH (Cumberland): Mr. Speaker, I rise to support the amendment moved by the hon. member for Queens-Lunen-burg (Mr. Ernst), and at the outset I should like to say that I see no useful purpose to be served in submitting this important question to a committee. That is what

The pension legislation of this country has been changed from time to time. First of all we had a board of pension commissioners; later on we had an additional body known as the federal appeal board. That body has not met the situation which confronts the ex-service men, nor has it been able to mete out justice to them or their dependents.
I appreciate the fact, as I think every member of the house does, that the resolution and amendment now under consideration will

War Pensions-Mr. Smith (Cumberland)
open the door very wide. Possibly it will lead to certain abuses and certainly it will be expensive; I think there is no question of that, but in my humble opinion it is the only policy that will do justice to the ex-service man. The question of cost, as has been stated several times to-day in this house, should not enter into the consideration of this matter. We have an obligation, a solemn duty to perform to the ex-service man; we must supply in pensions the physical deficiency which has resulted from his service during the war. That is our obligation, be the cost what it may, and we would fail in the discharge of our duty if in any degree we fell short of attaining that result. One of the hon. gentlemen opposite remarked this afternoon that possibly this might lift the lid off the treasury of the Dominion. In answer to that I think it might be said that we should tear the masks off the members of this house with regard to their attitude towards this problem. What would be the use of having a committee sitting again for several weeks and bringing back to this house the same recommendations as were brought back two years ago? Unless that committee recommended the very principle involved in the resolution and amendment we would be no better off than we are now. I suppose when the committee is in operation they would call the representatives of the ex-service men before them, in order to formulate certain suggestions with respect to routine procedure, departmental regulations, and other important phases of this matter which will have to be dealt with; but to my mind the principle of shifting the onus of proof must and should be established by this house in order that justice be done the returned soldiers. Every member who has spoken expressed deep consideration for the ex-service man and his 
dependents, and it seems to me that we should get away from all these technicalities and picayune points of procedure and at least establish a principle on which the Board of Pension Commissioners can successfully work, one which will operate fairly and justly to all ex-service men and their dependents in this country.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have listened with a great deal of interest to the discussion which has so far taken place on the resolution introduced by the hon. member for Muskoka-Ontario (Mr. McGibbon) and the amendment introduced by the hon. member for Queens-Lunenburg (Mr. Ernst).
I feel siure that no subject which could be brought before this house at the present time could be of more interest to the people of Canada than that which is now under consideration. It has been a source of great pleasure to me to observe the unanimity of opinion which exists among the members of this house who have taken part thus far in the discussion, that the ex-service man should receive the very greatest consideration which it is possible to give him. There seems to be also the feeling that in some measure the consideration which has been given to the exservice man in the past has not fully coped with the situation. I feel certain that no hon. member of this house will be satisfied until legislation has been framed which will give the ex-service man and his dependents the fullest possible consideration of their claims. The men who served this country so ably during the trying days from 1914 to 1918 believed that this country wTas prepared to stand by them, and they must be assured that parliament to-day is fully prepared to do its part.
It is not simply a matter of measuring out a dole to the ex-service men; we should give them sufficient or even more than sufficient to meet their present needs. Every hon. member of this house who is of the medical profession-in fact I am sure I can say practically every member, whether of the medical profession or not-has met with perhaps scores of cases of men who are not receiving under the present operation of the act the consideration to which they are entitled. As far as the Board of Pension Commissioners are concerned, in common with the other members who have spoken here, I have always found them just and fair and willing to cooperate to the fullest possible extent in securing for our ex-service men everything to which they were entitled under the operation of the present act. Unfortunately that act

War Pensions-Mr. Cotnam
has become 'hedged about with a certain amount of red tape and legal technicality which has made it inoperable when applied to a great number of our ex-service men. It is my hope that legislation will be introduced, following the lines of this resolution and the proposed amendment, which will deal more efficiently with those cases which do not come under the old Pension Act.
I have in mind a man who enlisted in 1916. He went overseas as an A-l man, served in five different units in France, was in hospital for a few days during the influenza epidemic of 1917-18, and returned to duty having a discharging ear. He mentioned this trouble to one of the men on duty at the hospital but was assured that although it frequently followed influenza it would clear up. Believing this to be the case he went back into the lines, but in later years this trouble has inoreased, and to-day, as a result of that condition. really acquired on active service, he is practically incapacitated from performing the duties of his ordinary vocation. On account of the fact that there are no records to show that this disability was acquired as a result of war service, this man is deprived of receiving the pension to which he is no doubt entitled. Medical men who are familiar with this type of case are willing, on their honour, to give certificates, but unfortunately the records do not provide the necessary information to show that the disability from which a man may now be suffering was acquired as a result of war service.
I most heartily endorse this resolution and the amendment which has been moved by the hon. member for Queens-Lunenburg. I feel sure that it will receive the most sympathetic consideration and will result in legislation being enacted which will take proper care of our ex-service men.

subtopic: DISABILITIES DUE TO WAR SERVICE-ONUS OP DISPROOF ON PENSION BOARD
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when the resolution of the hon. member for Muskoka-Ontario (Mr. McGibbon) and the amendment to that resolution by the hon. member for Queens-Lunenburg (Mr. Ernst) were being discussed this afternoon, I listened, as I am sure every hon. member of this house did, to the very interesting and illuminating addresses upon this very important question. Perhaps I may be permitted to give the impression which has been made upon my mind by these various speeches.
I recall an incident which occurred during my residence in New Zealand. For many years red clover would not grow in that country for more than one season. Efforts were made to have a second crop but they were of no avail, until a professor in one of
the universities discovered a remedy. To the professors in the various universities throughout the Dominion I must pay the honour of saying that they have made possible some of the greatest steps which have been taken in the progress of development, transcending even the work of this House of Commons. By examining the red clover through a microscope this gentleman discovered that the fertilization depended upon the native bee, but he discovered also that the tongue of that bee was not long enough to dip into the deep receptacle of the red clover and thus obtain the pollen to be distributed to other plants. Now, what did he do? He advised the New Zealand government to introduce into that country the large bumble bees of other countries. The result was that with the introduction of those bees the red clover became fertilized, produced seed, and laid the foundation of a wonderful growth of red clover in New Zealand.
The lesson I want to bring home is this: that the fault was not that of the red clover or of the climate or of the soil conditions; all depended for success on the tongue of the bee. I wish to make an application of that true story. We to-night in this house have before us something of great importance and the issue depends exactly not on the tongue of a bee but on the tongue of each member of the house. When we come to make a decision regarding the great body of soldiers who are not befitting by the provisions of soldiers' civil reestablishment or the operation of the pension board; when we are asked the question-and it is a question of right-are they entitled to come under the benefits of the act, we must use our tongues and say "yes" or "no".
Therefore, I want to present to-night a picture which, I think, should be presented on behalf of that body of men who are reticent and incapable of presenting their own cases before this tribunal. I am sure that everybody in Canada at one time or another has asked himself or herself why so large a number of returned soldiers are still unable to receive pensions or assistance under the provisions of soldiers' civil reestablishment or the operations of the pension board. Many books have been written and many articles have appeared in magazines giving vivid pictures of the life led in the trenches, of the heroism, the agony of mind and soul, the gradual physical, moral, social and emotional decay which make up in a great measure the story of the soldier's life in the great war. The returned soldier, as I said a moment ago, is reticent in speaking about what he underwent. He seems to despair of making one who

War Pensions-Mr. Brady

was not at the front see the first elements of that world he went through. The world the soldier went through in the great war is as incapable of explanation to those who were not there as the law of gravitation on a planet would be to one who had never seen or lived on it. The soldier's experience is not an arm-chair experience, and last evening I regretted deeply to hear what fell from the lips of one who should know more of human life and human temptation than he showed in his remarks, relative to a class of soldiers who fell by the wayside in that great conflict; because at this moment in Canada the experiences of that great conflict are still found pulsating through the arteries of the returned soldiers, loading their minds with a weight of memories of things seen, heard and suffered. The soldier's life to-day can never be what it was before he entered the theatre of war.
May I for a moment give the house a picture of what every day and every moment arises with recurring force in the minds of the men who have returned from the war? What do they see? In vision they see companions blown to pieces before their eyes. They see the crimson-streaked mud of the trenches. They see the filth, the poison gas, and they hear the unceasing din that shakes the soul out of the body into death. I wish to bring this picture to-night before the house in order to make a plea on behalf of the men who have not in their possession that personal history which is required before the present pension board.
I may be asked why it was that these men have delayed so long in presenting their cases to the pension board. In reply I would ask: Why was it that these men held together? What was it that kept them sane, that prompted them to such magnificent endurance and effort in the great war? The returned soldier to-day is lacking in that vital force which enabled him to endure and keep secret in his heart the troubles, physical, mental and spirituel, which he went through. What was that force? It was comradeship. When these men attempted to return to their vocations, the great strength and force of comradeship was absent from them. The result was that they were left with memories, with that which breaks down the spirit and the body, as it does, but to a lesser extent, even in civil life. The effect produced upon the men who returned, not wounded physically, but in many cases otherwise wounded more deeply, was often as severe, because of the tragedy through which they had passed, as if they had suffered bodily injury. I have under my hand a magazine, handed to me under one of those fortuitous circumstances which one meets with who loves

to visit the splendid reading room that is to be found within this House of Commons. There is in -this magazine an article written recently, which has made a profound impression on me, and it is appropriate that I should quote from it one paragraph. I feel that I should be demiss in my duty did I not -try to bring before this parliament the great need that exists to-day to ameliorate the living conditions of a great body of men who are not in a position to have their cases settled by the Board of Pension Commissioners, and there are many of them. Do you mean to tell me, Mr. Speaker, that the soldiers who fought through -the war did not suffer and are not suffering simply because they were not wounded on the battlefield? This book deals with a yoyng soldier who returned home after serving four years at the front. He enlisted with youths, found hopes vibrating in his blood. He left with great ambition. He saw scholarships ahead of him. He loved life; he loved nature; he loved everything. What was his condition on his return? He enters his library. He sees the things that once he knew and loved, and here are his words as he enters:
Nothing stirs: listless and wretched, like a condemned man. I sit there and the past withdraws itself. And at the same time I fear to importune it too much, because, I do not know what might haipen then. I am a soldier, I must cling to that. Wearily I stand up and look out of the window. Then I take one of the books, intending to read, and turn over the leaves. But I put it away and take out another. There are passages in it that have been marked. I look, turn over the pages, take up fresh books. Already they are piled up beside me. Speedily more join the heap, papers, magazines, letters. I stand there dumb. As before a judge. Dejected. Words, Words, Words-they do not reach me. Slowly I place the books back in the shelves. Nevermore. Quietly, I go out of the room.
That man's world, the world that he knew and belonged to, was dead to him. Is it any wonder, Mr. Speaker, that we experience a thrill when we think of the memories that lie in the hearts of the men who are appealing to us to-day to come to their rescue? Listen to this quotation-terrible are the words, but frightful are the memories, and it is essential that we should know wha.t lies in the minds and the hearts of the men who are seeking our aid to-day:
"He has been blown out of his clothes."
It is a soldier speaking to another of a companion:
"It's funny," replied his companion, "we have seen that a couple of times now. If a mortar gets you it blows you almost clean out of your clothes. Its the concussion that does it." I search round. And so it is. Here hang bits of uniform, and somewhere else is plastered a

War Pensions-Mr. Brady
bloody mess that was once a human limb. Over there lies a body with nothing but a piece of the underpants on one leg and the collar of the tunic around its neck. Otherwise it is naked and the clothes are hanging up in the tree. Both arms are missing as though they had been pulled out. I discover one of them twenty yards off in a shrub. The dead man lies on his face. There where the arm wounds are, the earth is black with blood. Underfoot the leaves are scratched up as though the man had been kicking.

speechtext: What is the hon. member quoting from, may I ask?

subtopic: DISABILITIES DUE TO WAR SERVICE-ONUS OP DISPROOF ON PENSION BOARD
speechtext:
I am quoting from an
English paper, the Spectator. I am trying to get before the house this simple thought, that there is a great body of our soldiers to-day' who are equally deserving of consideration bv the pensions board, by the federal appeal board, and by this government, but they are not able to come in under the law as it stands. How are we going to get them in? I heard it said during this debate that it is not possible to bring these men in under the Pension Act as it stands to-day, but I ask this house, is it not possible to make a change in the law which will allow them to come in and receive the benefits to which they are equally entitled with other pensioners? It is not a question of sending this important matter to a committee. The committee question is not one that should be considered in a grave issue. I heard it stated this evening: This is not a political question. Why should it be? Why should it be even hinted that the interests of our returned soldiers who fought for Canada and the empire should be submitted to any party or to any particular class that should make a political question of it? That should not be, Mr. Speaker, and I trust tha-t there is no intention in this house to make it a political question.
I want to bring home the fact that the psychology underlying the story of the returned soldier is one of profound importance. I shall never forget an incident in my own life. It was a simple thing that has no doubt a parallel in the lives of many in this house. I was called upon at a very unexpected moment and under the most adverse weather conditions-it was in mid-winter-to jump from my boat, going at six knots an hour in an open harbour, far from the shore line, to save the life of my child. I did not hesitate. Then, forgetful of everything, whether I wore heavy clothing or not, I jumped from that moving boat and succeeded in getting my little daughter. May I tell this house that profound truths can be sought and found regarding the major problems of life from the minor
2419- lOi
ones which concern us as individuals. What did I find, sir, when I looked around in those turbulent waters? I found myself far removed from help. I sought the nearest point of land and with endless trouble I reached the goal that I desired to reach, and I saved my child. What was the result? I did not feel any sensation of weakness, but rather joy in the fact that I had accomplished the work which I had set out to do. Let me tell you, sir, that one month later the memory of that tragedy, or at least what might have been a tragedy, was so overpowering to me that I simply broke down, my nervous system was undermined, and it took a whole year for me to recover. That was my experience. But, Mr. Speaker, what must be the experience of men who went through four years of hell at the front, who saw and took part in that terrible carnage and now are beginning to feel the baleful effects? I noticed that to-night the hon. member for Southeast Grey (Miss Macphail) seemed, as it were, to understand exactly what- the returned soldier feels when she said that many of these men to-day are old in body but young in years. Yes, sir, they are old in body though young in years.
But is it possible that we are forgetful of what took place a few years ago when our young men went out to war from a high sense of duty, when they left all that was near and dear to them? We should be grateful to them and try to solve their problems, not simply touch their minor difficulties and present them for amelioration. I think that the mover of this resolution has helped us as a body to come together and show a united front in regard to our returned men. I come from a large constituency. It is not like Toronto, or Montreal, or Vancouver. I travel thousands of miles through my constituency where returned soldiers are now established, and I should like to picture to this house the heroic struggles of those men to rehabilitate themselves in the civil life. It would surprise hon. members to know what those men are doing. The great body of men for whom we are asking consideration have had the courage to get back to civil life from the demoralizing effects of war, believing they could carry out their civilian duties as they did before the war. That being the case, why should these men be kept outside the door which, once opened, will enable them to benefit a little in this great period of social progress?
I have in mind one or two cases, Mr. Speaker, which I think are typical of the thousands which could be presented to this house. I recall a boy who left for the front at eighteen years of age. He was a university
War Pensions-Mr. Ryckman

graduate and training to become a civil engineer. Unfortunately for himself, perhaps, he was not wounded physically; but he was wounded in soul and in mind. After three years' service he came back and was given a position in a post office, the only position available, bait he could not hold that position owing to the noise in the office, which brought on serious mental trouble. Later he sought a position on the Canadian National Railways. He was given a good position, one that would have suited him admirably had he been physically fit. But what happened? After a month or two he found himself unable to retain it. To-day that young man cannot present to the pension board a medical history that would warrant the granting of a pension.
I hope and trust, sir, that this resolution as amended may meet with hearty support from every part of this house, and that once for all our soldiers' claims will receive that consideration and kindness to which they are entitled.
Hon. E.B. RYCKMAN (East Toronto): Mr. Speaker, I have no excuse to offer for intervening in this debate at 'this fete hour. I desire to support the principle of the resolution and of the amendment. I aim anxious to know wbait the right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) and his government hove to propose in view of What is suggested on this side of the house. This morning I picked up my newspaper and read that the United States had just appropriated an extra one hundred million dollars for pensions.

Per year, as I am informed. I do not think the United States had more war casualties 'than Canada. I hope it will not be necessary for us to set aside any such sum, but we have the assurance of those who have spoken on the other side that, to quote the very words, "All are agreed that something should be done." That was said by the member for Lisgar (Mr. Brown). "Something should be done." In view of what has been said on the other side of the house, I think that is a fair statement. Now what is that something? To this question I have given a great deal of consideration, the best that I could, and I want to tell the house now that there is no other thing that can be done by this house, or by a committee of this house, or by those who are interested in the welfare of the soldiers than to shift the onus of proof. I want this house to mark that; that come out of this discussion as we may, let this house resolve as it desires to do, and you will find that in the
TMr. Brady.]
interests of the soldier you must shift the onus of proof. And yet the government allow those on its side to get aip and say that this would shake the basic principles of law and evidence. How ridiculous! The member for AVdnnipeg South Centre (Mr. Thorson) spoke, and did he approve Of thaj;? Did he contradict it as a lawyer? No not a word to say. The member for Hants-Kings (Mr. Usley) spoke. Did anyone support the statement that we were smashing through the basic principles of law and evidence? No one supported it, but they did not care to correct the feeling expressed in the house by some who did not know but that perhaps there might be something in it. There was nothing.
The next thing that.was attempted was to find some fault with the resolution as it stood at first. It was not drawn by a lawyer, we are told, and there was nothing wrong with it; it was right in every particular. Then' someone objected-I think it was the Solicitor General (Mr. Cannon)-to the word "disproof" which is the proper word to use in the circumstances.

Well, I accept the
hon. gentleman's statement, 'but someone over there very near to the Solicitor General was very much exercised over this word "disproof". I refer him to Murray's dictionary and to Webster's dictionary I shall not take time to go into that.
Then the statement was made-wholly incorrect-that this was a means of getting pensions by way of a dishonest doctor. Nothing in it at all. What was the situation? It was this, as stated in the resolution as it originally stood, that if a man whio had been overseas-the first point, overseas-had been in a theatre of war, had served, came 'back, was afflicted and then showed by evidence or by the opinion of a reputable doctor, which of course is expert evidence, that there was a connection between the disability and the overseas service, then he was entitled to a pension unless it could (be shown that he was not so entitled. (Suppose the (testimony was *that Of one doctor. That testimony would be met if there was another doctor who said: my opinion is contrary to that expressed by the one who has just spoken on behalf of the *returned man. That would bet balance. Then if 'there was further 'testimony it would be a question of weighing it and determining which was right, whether there should be pension or whether there should not be pension.
Take this case, and I see an hon. member in the house who is very familiar with it. There

Natural Resources-Agreements
is a returned soldier who is working in a mine. You have been interested in mines and minerals; you know this man, and you have a curio in the shape of a piece of unsmelted ore. You hand P to him; he appreciates your gift and takes it home. The mine authorities find out that he has that piece of unsmelted ore in 'his home. What is the law? The law made by the parliament of Canada is that that man is prima facie a thief until he .proves that he came by that unsmelted ore honestly. Is it fair that the l'aw should be thus in that case and unfair for the returned soldier to say to Canada: Well, you took me abroad in the war; it may be that I wanted to go, but I served you as well as I could; I came home and I am troubled by reason of what I suffered over there; the presumption is on you to show that you in your generous treatment of others should not treat me in the same way.
Oh, the cases are many. There is a member, I won't say on which side of the house he may be. He has some poker chips in his house, I have not any. Someone says he thinks there is gambling going on in that house and that men lose their money. All you have to do is to make that affirmation; the officers go to the house and find the poker chips, or the roulette wheel, and the owner of that house has to prove that it is not a common gaming house. The onus is on him; and, further, those who are in the house are presumed to be frequenters until they show that they are not. And then we are told, with a waste of much energy and gesticulation, at that end of the house, that it is a breach of the principles of law and evidence! As was said here by the hon. gentleman who introduced the resolution, the liquor act is the same way, the highways act is the same way in the province of Ontario, and there are other cases.
Suppose there is a brand upon cattle,-this will be of interest to western members of parliament,.-and that cattle is found in my barnyard. It is presumed that that cattle belongs to the owner of the brand and I have to prove how I got it. And yet so jealous are hon. gentlemen opposite to preserve the basic principles of law and evidence that they say it would be a shaking of the conscience if in respect to a soldier who had gone abroad, had served and suffered, had returned and was afflicted, it should then be the duty of the country who took him to prove that his ills were not caused by his service.
